scope: Orders 15–32 of docs/design/odysseys/new-rome.json; read-only source-access and factual audit. No episode, chronology, map, or design changed.

episodes.place: Antioch on the Orontes; exact sack footprint within the city not established.

sources.locator: Procopius, Persian Wars II.8–10
sources.consulted: The cited page and adjacent text were checked; the source narrates Khosrow’s expedition, Antioch’s capture and sack, fire, and deportation of captives.
sources.supports: Supports capture/sack and forced removal as Procopius’ account of the 540 campaign.
sources.limits: Near-contemporary author but literary, dramatic narrative; casualty/captive numbers and details are not independently confirmed here. Page notes Loeb text public domain, but reuse/licensing of site presentation and images not established.

sources.locator: Sarah Savant? article “God’s Wrath over Antioch 525–540 CE”
sources.consulted: Search result/metadata only; full article text was not read.
sources.supports: A modern scholarly lead for interpreting Procopius and the Antioch disasters.
sources.limits: Cannot treat abstract/search excerpt as verification of its detailed argument; full access not established. Copyright/reuse unknown.

episodes.assessment: Core event is supported as Procopius’ account; keep numbers and localized destruction qualified, and avoid fabricating civilian testimony.

episodes.date: 542 CE; plague in Constantinople lasted four months according to Procopius (episode date is within this plague crisis).

sources.locator: Procopius, Persian Wars II.22.9; II.23.1–20
sources.consulted: Opened full translated section. II.22.9 says the plague reached Byzantium in spring of its second year; II.23.1 gives four months/three months at greatest virulence; II.23.5–8 says Justinian provided money and assigned Theodorus to bury unattended dead; II.23.19 explicitly reports near-starvation and difficulty obtaining bread/necessities.
sources.supports: Directly supports plague, imperial relief for burial, mortality/disruption, and scarcity of bread/necessities in the city.
sources.limits: Procopius’ supernatural explanations, moral judgments, and reported daily death tolls are authorial testimony, not verified counts. It does not prove an actual empty public granary or a specific rationing scheme. Site labels 1914 translation public domain; site images/reuse still governed separately.

sources.locator: Byzantium overview, Justinian/plague context
sources.consulted: Page opened; overview inspected, not a dedicated food-distribution study.
sources.supports: Broad Byzantine chronology and material-culture context only.
sources.limits: Does not substantiate a particular granary, supply route, or allocation event. Museum text rights should be checked before reuse.

episodes.assessment: The shortage detail is better grounded in Procopius than in the selected Met overview; player allocation remains fictional.

episodes.place: Constantinople; exact meeting building not established by consulted passage.

sources.locator: Second Council of Constantinople, Session I imperial letter and acts
sources.consulted: Opened and read opening acts. The imperial letter states the controversy over the Three Chapters and calls bishops to the capital; later acts/decrees in the collection address Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret’s anti-Cyril writings, and the letter attributed to Ibas.
sources.supports: Supports a council convened at Constantinople in 553 and condemnation of the Three Chapters.
sources.limits: This translated ecclesiastical dossier preserves partisan theological and imperial framing. The same opening says Vigilius would not attend the common synod, so the council’s relationship with the pope is contested/complex; “uneven reception” needs region-specific evidence. It does not establish a specific city venue. Reproduction rights for the modern webpage/translation not checked.

episodes.assessment: The central event is supported by the acts, while the official unity narrative should not be treated as evidence of uniform reception.

episodes.place: Constantinople; Avars on the European side, Persian forces across the Bosporus at Chalcedon in the Christian homiletic account.

sources.locator: Theodore Syncellus, Homily on the siege, sections describing the Avar approach and Persian position
sources.consulted: Opened and read the translated homily. It describes the Avar khagan’s attack from the west and Persians across the strait at Chalcedon, with land/sea pressure on the city.
sources.supports: Primary/near-contemporary panegyric supports a 626 Avar attack and separate Persian presence across the water; supports the distinction that Persians were not a same-bank combined siege force.
sources.limits: Christian homily is celebratory and polemical (including anti-Avar and anti-Jewish rhetoric); supernatural explanation and enemy figures are not neutral evidence. Ferry logistics/supply specifics were not verified. Textual dating/attribution has scholarly discussion; copyright of hosted translation not verified.

sources.locator: Siege of Constantinople (626), overview
sources.consulted: Page identified through citation; its full text was not accessible/read in this audit.
sources.supports: Secondary reference lead only.
sources.limits: Do not mark as directly consulted evidence; primary homily above supports the qualified geography. Reuse rights unknown.

episodes.assessment: The geographic distinction between Avar and Persian positions matters; exact strength, miraculous interventions, and detailed ferry/supply scenes remain unverified.

episodes.date: 637/638 CE; dates in later accounts vary.

sources.locator: Robert G. Hoyland, Witnesses to a World Crisis, chapter abstract/extract on seventh-century eastern Christian sources
sources.consulted: Opened only the accessible chapter abstract/extract. It places Arab campaigns from 634, gives Ajnadayn 634, Fihl 634/635, Yarmuk 636 and says Jerusalem arranged surrender terms perhaps in 638.
sources.supports: Supports the broad conquest context and explicitly qualifies Jerusalem’s surrender date as perhaps 638.
sources.limits: Full chapter not consulted; abstract cannot support detailed property provisions or local encounter narratives. Copyright/reuse unknown.

sources.limits: Not treated as passage read; later chronicle transmission is not a contemporary surrender act. Access and rights unknown.

sources.consulted: The cited page was not opened/read in this session.

sources.limits: Do not use it as evidence for capitulation. Translation/editorial rights not checked.

episodes.date: Conventional c.674–678 date disputed; alternative reconstructions place related operations in the later 660s or reject a continuous siege.
episodes.place: Constantinople and surrounding eastern Mediterranean; no specific operation site fixed by this audit.

sources.locator: Critical overview of the first Arab siege debate; discussion of Theophanes, Howard-Johnston, Jankowiak
sources.consulted: Read from the cited page/summary during prior audit; it contrasts major scholarly reconstructions and stresses source-chronology problems.
sources.supports: Supports that a continuous 674–678 siege is disputed and that Theophanes’ chronology/source use is problematic.
sources.limits: This is a secondary explainer, not primary or peer-reviewed final authority. Howard-Johnston’s “no siege” and Jankowiak’s earlier siege reconstruction differ materially. A clear event should be described as contested Arab-Byzantine operations, not certain four-year blockade. Exact Greek-fire deployment and naval location not verified. Copyright/reuse unknown.

sources.locator: Arab-Byzantine wars overview
sources.consulted: Cited page identified; full page not read in this pass.
sources.supports: Background lead only.
sources.limits: Cannot by itself resolve the contested chronology; no primary passage was opened for the conventional siege.

episodes.assessment: Strong caveat: the date range and even “siege” as a continuous event are disputed; do not portray an exact naval blockade chronology as settled.

episodes.place: Constantinople; council proceedings, specific meeting room unverified.

sources.supports: Theophanes supports the conventional siege narrative and its winter/Bulgar elements as a Byzantine chronicle account.
sources.limits: Chronicle written later and politically/theologically framed; numerical casualties, exact one-year chronology, and causal primacy of Bulgarian aid are not secure. Different source traditions diverge. Translation rights unknown.

sources.supports: Supports broad iconoclast controversy under Leo III and chronology as a scholarly issue.
sources.limits: Abstract cannot establish a particular decree, artisan incident, or workshop protection. The often-asserted 726/730 imperial edict is disputed; images policy evolved rather than a single securely documented act. Full chapter access failed. Rights unknown.

sources.supports: Indirectly supports that Hieria promulgated an iconoclast definition and was later rejected at Nicaea II.
sources.limits: This is a hostile later reconstruction, not neutral surviving acts of 754. Do not treat workshop logistics or local civilian consequences as sourced by this council text. Reuse rights not checked.

sources.limits: Does not expose primary text or event logistics.

sources.supports: Supports the council’s doctrinal position and the veneration/latria distinction.
sources.limits: Acts are an ecclesiastical/theological record; translation terms vary. Do not equate the 787 formulation with modern denominational identities. Detailed local memory/story is not established by the acts. Rights for modern translation/site not checked.

sources.consulted: URL identified in selection; cited chapter was not extracted/read during this pass. Prior audit recorded only the candidate claim from metadata.

episodes.assessment: Coronation is conventional, but the cited witness and its famously dramatic “surprise” explanation remain to be checked directly.

sources.supports: Supports broad chronology of restoration in 843.
sources.limits: Not primary evidence; full chapter unavailable. “Triumph of Orthodoxy” is source/tradition language, not an unchanging modern institutional label.

sources.consulted: Search result inspected; describes later icon image of the restoration subject and an 18th-century painter’s manual.
sources.supports: Supports later visual reception of the 843 event as a remembered subject.
sources.limits: The object is much later than 843 and cannot document contemporary scene details; image rights/licence need checking before reuse.

episodes.assessment: The 843 policy reversal and later commemoration are supported at broad level; do not treat later iconography as contemporary eyewitness evidence.

crossEpisodeFindings: Procopius II.22–23 directly supports plague-related mortality, burial relief and scarcity in Constantinople; the episode’s specific granary remains fictional.
Several selected references are abstracts or inaccessible pages. They are marked explicitly and must not be cited as full-text verification.
The 626 homily distinguishes Avar attack from the Persian position across the strait; numbers and panegyrical/miraculous claims remain attributed.
The supposed 674–678 continuous siege is strongly contested in modern source criticism; even the event’s duration/date is unresolved.
The 754 Hieria acts and several eighth/ninth-century narratives survive here through later, interested witnesses.
Pliska and Versinikia are regional battle identifications in this audit, not precise geolocated battlefield footprints.
No map/image asset was downloaded; asset reuse rights/licences remain unknown unless the source explicitly identifies public-domain text.
accessAndReuse: Access labels distinguish full passage read, prior-pass reading, abstract/preview/metadata, unconsulted and failed access. Do not claim full-book access from an abstract. Procopius page explicitly labels 1914 Loeb text public domain; web presentation/images have separate rights. All other translation, article, museum-image and map licences remain unverified; obtain rights before reusing assets.
